question: Why do we use standard precautions in the hospital?

options.B: To reduce the cost of patient care supplies
options.C: To prevent the transmission of infectious agents
options.D: To eliminate all microorganisms from the hospital environment

explanation: Spot on! Standard precautions are our everyday shield. By treating all body fluids as potentially infectious, we stop germs from spreading between patients and healthcare workers.

question: Which part of the chain of infection do standard precautions target the most?
explanation: You got it! Barriers like gloves, masks, and hand hygiene cut off the travel route, stopping pathogens from moving from the source to the patient or nurse.

question: When must you use soap and water instead of an alcohol-based hand rub?

options.B: At the beginning and end of a nursing shift
options.C: When working in the emergency department
options.D: When hands are visibly soiled with dirt or body fluids

explanation: Correct! Alcohol rubs are great, but they cannot cut through visible dirt or grime. When your hands look or feel dirty, good old soap and water is a must.

question: How long should you rub your hands together when using an alcohol-based hand rub?
explanation: That is correct! Taking at least 20 to 30 seconds ensures you cover all surfaces of your hands and give the sanitizer enough time to kill the germs.

question: When should you wear medical gloves while caring for a patient?

options.C: During all routine vital sign measurements
options.D: When anticipating contact with blood or body fluids

explanation: Spot on! Wear gloves whenever there is a chance your hands might touch blood, body fluids, mucous membranes, or broken skin.

question: You are about to irrigate a wound and expect fluid to splash. What PPE do you need?

options.B: Gloves, a gown, and eye protection with a mask
options.C: A sterile surgical cap and shoe covers

explanation: You nailed it! Whenever a procedure is messy and likely to splash, protect your hands, skin, clothes, and face with full barrier gear.

question: What is the safest thing to do right after giving an injection with a disposable syringe?

options.A: Place the uncapped syringe on the patient's bedside table
options.B: Drop the entire syringe into a nearby sharps container
options.C: Recap the needle firmly using a two-handed technique
options.D: Break the needle off before disposal

explanation: Correct! To avoid accidental needle pricks, always drop the whole sharp device straight into a puncture-resistant container without trying to recap it.

question: Why is it dangerous to overfill a sharps container in the ward?

options.A: It slows down the disposal of regular paper waste
options.B: It increases the risk of accidental needle puncture injuries
options.C: It releases toxic fumes into the clinical area
options.D: It causes the plastic container to melt

explanation: Spot on! Sticking needles out of an overfilled box is an accident waiting to happen for nurses, doctors, and cleaning staff.

question: What is the recommended alternative if a patient with a cough does not have a tissue available?

options.A: Covering the mouth with a shared towel
options.C: Turning their head toward the nurse
options.D: Coughing directly into their bare hands

explanation: Coughing into the elbow prevents respiratory droplets from contaminating the hands, which easily transfer germs to surfaces and other people. [learn more](GNS112_U5_T11#GNS112_U5_T11_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT part of basic respiratory hygiene in a clinic waiting area?

options.A: Placing hand sanitizer dispensers near the entrance
options.B: Mandating full isolation gowns for all visitors
options.D: Offering surgical masks to coughing individuals

explanation: Correct! Visitors do not need isolation gowns just to sit in a waiting area. Respiratory hygiene is all about masks, tissues, clean hands, and catching coughs.

question: When should reusable items like a blood pressure cuff be disinfected?

options.B: Once at the end of each nursing shift
options.C: Only when visibly stained with blood
options.D: Once a week during deep cleaning

explanation: Spot on! To stop cross-contamination between patients, always clean and disinfect reusable equipment after every single use.

question: Why must you follow the manufacturer's 'contact time' when using disinfectant wipes?

options.A: It stops the chemical from smelling unpleasant
options.B: It ensures the chemical has enough time to kill the pathogens
options.C: It prevents the plastic equipment from scratching
options.D: It makes the wipe dry faster in humid rooms

explanation: You got it! Disinfectants need to stay wet on a surface for a specific number of minutes to actually destroy stubborn bacteria and viruses.

question: What is the very first thing you should do if you accidentally get a needle stick injury?

options.A: Wait until the end of the shift to report it
options.B: Squeeze the finger to drain as much blood as possible
options.C: Wash the affected area immediately with soap and water
options.D: Apply an antibiotic ointment and a bandage

explanation: Correct! Wash the spot right away with soap and water to wash away as many germs as possible before they enter your bloodstream.

question: A glass bottle of lab specimen drops and shatters on the floor, creating a large spill. What should you do first?

options.A: Cover the glass shards with a cloth sheet
options.B: Leave the room and wait for the housekeeping staff to notice
options.C: Put on appropriate PPE and obtain a designated spill kit
options.D: Mop the floor quickly with a dry paper towel

explanation: Spot on! Safety first: always wear your PPE before dealing with broken glass and body fluids to protect yourself from exposure.
